questiontext.text:
Solve \({@eqd@}\) for \(0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ\). Give angles that are not whole numbers to 1 decimal place.

\(x \in\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Replace \(\cos^2 x\) by \(1 - \sin^2 x\) and write \(s = \sin x\). Collecting terms gives \({@qd@}\).

Its roots are \(s = {@dispdp(float(sb),4)@}\) and \(s = {@dispdp(float(sv),4)@}\) (to 4 decimal places: use the formula if the quadratic does not factorise). \(\sin x\) can never be bigger than 1 or smaller than \(-1\), so \(\sin x = {@dispdp(float(sb),4)@}\) is rejected.

\(\sin x = {@dispdp(float(sv),4)@}\): the calculator gives \({@setraw(calc)@}\). [[if test="is(sv > 0)"]]Sine is also positive in the second quadrant, at \(180^\circ\) minus that angle.[[else]]Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants: use \(180^\circ\) plus and \(360^\circ\) minus the size of that angle.[[/if]] So \(x \in {@setraw(sols)@}\).

questiondescription.text:
Trigonometry III: solving a quadratic trigonometric equation

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.5: Solve p cos^2 x + q sin x + r = 0 for 0 to 360 degrees using the identity, rejecting the impossible root; some variants need the quadratic formula.

Core

This question is adapted from Example 9 in Section E and Question 7 in Test yourself of Chapter 7 of Cassell, D., Instone, S., Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP AS/A2 Mathematics: Core 2 for AQA, Cambridge University Press, 2004: the sine form in degrees with new equations, randomised over a curated list, with the answer typed as a set and named feedback added.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(sv > 0)"]]

{@setstr(calc)@} is the angle your calculator gives, and it is a solution. Another angle between \(0^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\) has the same sine: use the symmetry of the sine graph to find it.

[[else]]

{@setstr(calc)@} is the angle your calculator gives, but it is outside \(0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ\). Two angles in the interval have the same sine, one in the third quadrant and one in the fourth: use the symmetry of the sine graph to find them.

[[/if]]
These come from \(\cos^2 x = \sin^2 x - 1\). The identity gives \(\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x\).

Every angle you gave is a solution, but the equation has {@length(solsF)@} solutions in \(0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ\) and you gave {@length(sl)@}.[[if test="miss360"]] When \(0^\circ\) is a solution, \(360^\circ\) is one too: both ends are in the interval.[[/if]]

[[if test="is(extras = [])"]]You have every solution, but you gave at least one of them twice, to different accuracy. Give each angle once.[[else]]You have every solution, but also {@setstr(extras)@}.[[/if]][[if test="is(outside # [])"]] Angles outside \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) are not wanted: add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring a calculator value into the interval.[[/if]]

Each of your angles is close to a solution, but not correct to 1 decimal place. Keep full calculator accuracy and round only at the end, to 1 decimal place (round up when the next digit is 5 or more).

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(resx # [])"]]

Test your angles in the equation. For the left side of the equation, {@resstr@}. A solution gives \(0\).

[[/if]]

Replace \(\cos^2 x\) by \(1 - \sin^2 x\), rearrange to a quadratic in \(\sin x\), solve it (use the formula if it does not factorise), reject any value outside \(-1\) to \(1\), then find both angles.

[[if test="is(outside # [])"]]

Angles outside \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) are not wanted: add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring a calculator value into the interval.

[[/if]][[if test="radn"]]

All your values are small: check that your calculator is in degree mode, and give angles in degrees.

[[/if]]
